facts.statement: Taniwhasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Campanian stage, with potential records from the Santonian stage in South Africa, Japan, and Russia.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian), Potential Santonian record in South Africa, Japan and Russia.

facts.statement: The genus Taniwhasaurus was first described by the Scottish naturalist James Hector in 1874.
facts.quote: authority: Hector, 1874

facts.statement: Two species are currently recognized within the genus: T. antarcticus described by Novas et al. in 2002 and T. mikasaensis described by Caldwell et al. in 2008.
facts.quote: subdivision: T. antarcticus (Novas et al., 2002) T. mikasaensis Caldwell et al., 2008

facts.statement: Taniwhasaurus is an extinct genus of marine lizards known as mosasaurs that lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Taniwhasaurus is an extinct genus of mosasaurs (a group of extinct marine lizards) that lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Taniwhasaurus was a medium-sized mosasaur with a maximum estimated length of around 6.7 meters.
facts.quote: Taniwhasaurus is a medium-sized mosasaurid, with maximum size estimates putting it at around 6.7 m in length.

facts.statement: CT scans of T. antarcticus suggest that Taniwhasaurus likely possessed an electro-sensitive organ capable of detecting prey movements underwater, similar to modern aquatic predators.
facts.quote: CT scans performed on the snout foramina of T. antarcticus show that Taniwhasaurus, like various aquatic predators today, would likely have had an electro-sensitive organ capable of detecting the movements of prey underwater.

facts.statement: The type species T. oweni was discovered in the 1860s in the Conway Formation at Haumuri Bluff in eastern New Zealand.
facts.quote: The first known species, Taniwhasaurus oweni, was discovered in the 1860s in the cliffs of Haumuri Bluff, located in the Conway Formation, eastern New Zealand.

facts.statement: The Conway Formation where T. oweni was found dates to the Upper Cretaceous, specifically the lower and middle Campanian stages.
facts.quote: This formation is dated from the Upper Cretaceous, more precisely from the lower and middle Campanian stage.

facts.statement: James Hector formally described the first fossils attributed to Taniwhasaurus in 1874.
facts.quote: The first fossils formally attributed to this taxon were described by the Scottish naturalist James Hector in 1874.

facts.statement: New material from Haumuri Bluff was discovered in 1999 and formally described by Michael W. Caldwell and colleagues in 2005.
facts.quote: In 1999 that new cranial and postcranial material was discovered in the cliffs of Haumuri Bluff and that these findings were formalized by Michael W. Caldwell and his colleagues in 2005.

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that Tylosaurus haumuriensis is a junior synonym of T. oweni because the differences between the two taxa are mainly due to size rather than distinct morphology.
facts.quote: Based on extensive analyzes of these fossils, researchers found that there are in fact few morphological differences between the two mosasaur taxa from this locality, the differences being mainly due to the larger size of specimen NMNZ R1532, making Tylosaurus haumuriensis a junior synonym of T. oweni.

facts.statement: Juan M. Lirio discovered a well-preserved mosasaur specimen in January 2000 on James Ross Island in Antarctica.
facts.quote: In January 2000, paleontologist Juan M. Lirio discovered a remarkably well-preserved specimen of a mosasaur in the Gamma Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation, located on James Ross Island in Antarctica.

facts.statement: The geological formation containing the Antarctic specimen dates from the late Campanian to late Maastrichtian stages of the Upper Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The Gamma Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation is dated in the late Campanian to late Maastrichtian stages of the Upper Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Fernando E. Novas and colleagues initially named the Antarctic specimen Lakumasaurus antarcticus.
facts.quote: After analyzing the material, Fernando E. Novas and his colleagues named it Lakumasaurus antarcticus.

facts.statement: James E. Martin questioned the validity of Lakumasaurus as a separate genus starting in 2006, suggesting the cranial features were too small to warrant a distinct genus.
facts.quote: From 2006, James E. Martin questioned the validity of Lakumasaurus as a separate genus, noting that the cranial features are small enough to justify such a proposal.

facts.statement: Subsequent studies have expressed skepticism regarding the claim that a juvenile skull found in the Maastrichtian belongs to T. antarcticus.
facts.quote: but subsequent studies are skeptical of this claim.

facts.statement: Fossils of Taniwhasaurus were first collected in the Pondoland region of South Africa at the beginning of the 20th century.
facts.quote: At the beginning of the 20th century, several fossils began to be collected in the region of Pondoland, in South Africa.

facts.statement: A set of fragmentary jawbone fossils catalogued as SAM-PK-5265 was initially attributed to a reptile related to the genus Mosasaurus in 1901.
facts.quote: In 1901, one of the sets of fossils discovered (catalogued as SAM-PK-5265), being a few fragmentary pieces of a jawbone, was referred as belonging to a reptile considered close to the genus Mosasaurus.

facts.statement: In 2016, Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro proposed reclassifying T. capensis into the genus Taniwhasaurus based on skull characteristics.
facts.quote: In 2016, Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro published a thesis which analyzes the deep relationships between the various tylosaurines. Based on observations of the specimen SAM-PK-5265, she proposes moving this species to Taniwhasaurus, claiming that the characteristics found there are closer to this latter than to Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2019, Jimenez-Huidobro and Caldwell maintained the proposal to place the species in Taniwhasaurus but noted the fossils were too poorly preserved for a definitive genus-level identification.
facts.quote: In 2019, Jimenez-Huidobro and Caldwell reaffirm this proposition, but found that the fossils were too poorly preserved to identify definitively to the genus.

facts.statement: A 2022 anatomical review concluded that the SAM-PK-5265 specimen is a chimera of two genera, with parts belonging to cf. Prognathodon and parts to cf. Taniwhasaurus, making species-level identification impossible.
facts.quote: In 2022, an anatomical review of South African mosasaurs analyzed SAM-PK-5265 and found the specimen to be a chimera of two different mosasaur genera, but not identifiable at the species level: the frontoparietal complex and the posterior dentary fragment without teeth represent cf. Prognathodon, while the anterior dentary fragment with replacement teeth represents cf. Taniwhasaurus.

facts.statement: The specimen was found in a floating concretion within the Kashima Formation of the Yezo Group in Hokkaido.
facts.quote: This specimen was found in a floating concretion, and its formation of origin was identified with the Kashima Formation, in the Yezo Group, the locality being the exposed area of this same place.

facts.statement: The formation containing the Taniwhasaurus specimen is dated to the Santonian-Campanian stage.
facts.quote: Like the previously mentioned sites, the formation from which the animal was found is dated to the Santonian-Campanian stage.

facts.statement: The specimen MCM.M0009 was informally named Yezosaurus mikasaensis in November 1976 and erroneously classified as a tyrannosauroid dinosaur in December 1976.
facts.quote: The specimen, cataloged MCM.M0009, was informally named "Yezosaurus mikasaensis" in a press release issued by Kikuwo Muramoto and Ikuwo Obata on November 30, 1976, before being erroneously classified as a tyrannosauroid dinosaur in an article published by Muramoto in December of the same year.

facts.statement: Caldwell and colleagues formally described the specimen as the new species Taniwhasaurus mikasaensis in 2008.
facts.quote: In 2008, Caldwell and colleagues formally redescribed the specimen as a new species of Taniwhasaurus, T. mikasaensis.

facts.statement: In 2019, Jimenez-Huidobro and Caldwell classified the specimen as an indeterminate species of Taniwhasaurus due to insufficient fossil material for a distinct species diagnosis.
facts.quote: In 2019, the phylogenetic revision of tylosaurines conducted by Jimenez-Huidobro and Calwell still considers the specimen to be a representative of the genus Taniwhasaurus, but the authors argued that the fossils are insufficient for a diagnosis to classify it as a distinct species, so they reclassified it as an indeterminate species of Taniwhasaurus.

facts.statement: Taniwhasaurus is considered a medium-sized mosasaur that was shorter than its relative Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: Although fossils of Taniwhasaurus are incomplete, existing remains suggest the genus was a medium-sized mosasaur shorter than its relative Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: The largest known specimen of T. oweni (SMU NMNZ R1532) has a skull length of 86.9 cm and an estimated total body length of 6.72 meters.
facts.quote: The largest known specimen of T. oweni is the partial skull specimen SMU NMNZ R1532, which was estimated to have measured 86.9 cm long, resulting in a total body length estimate of 6.72 m.

facts.statement: T. antarcticus is a smaller species with a holotype skull length of 72 cm.
facts.quote: Table S1 T. antarcticus represents a smaller species, with the holotype having a skull length of 72 cm.

facts.statement: The skull of Taniwhasaurus is triangular in shape when viewed from above.
facts.quote: In dorsal view, the skull of Taniwhasaurus is triangular in shape.

facts.statement: The skull of Taniwhasaurus features an edentulous rostrum, an anterior process of the dentary bone, and the frontal bone excluded from the orbit margin.
facts.quote: Like other tylosaurines, the skull of is characterized by the presence of an edentulous rostrum, an anterior process to the dentary bone, and an exclusion of the frontal from the margin of the orbit.

facts.statement: The snout of T. oweni is straight, whereas the snout of T. antarcticus is curved.
facts.quote: The snout of T. oweni is rather straight, while in T. antarcticus it is curved.

facts.statement: The premaxilla of Taniwhasaurus has a longitudinal crest on its anterior dorsal surface, unlike the smooth dorsal surface found in Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: The premaxilla of Taniwhasaurus bears a longitudinal crest on the anterior half of its dorsal surface, unlike that of Tylosaurus in which the dorsal surface of the premaxilla is smooth.

facts.statement: The mandible of Taniwhasaurus is slender and features an unusually high coronoid process.
facts.quote: The mandible of Taniwhasaurus is characterized for having a slender structure and an unusually high coronoid process.

facts.statement: T. oweni has 14 maxillary teeth, while T. antarcticus has 12.
facts.quote: In the maxillary teeth, T. oweni has 14, while T. antarcticus has 12.

facts.statement: T. oweni has 15 dentary teeth, while T. antarcticus has 13.
facts.quote: At the level of the dentary bones, T. oweni has 15 teeth, while T. antarcticus has 13.

facts.statement: Both T. oweni and T. antarcticus have only 2 teeth in the premaxillae.
facts.quote: In both species there are only 2 teeth in the premaxillae.

facts.statement: The neural spine of the axis vertebra is stout and elongated, ending in a broad, flattened spike that likely supported a cartilaginous cap.
facts.quote: The neural spine of the axis is stout and elongated, culminating posterodorsally in a broad, flattened, incomplete spike that probably bore a cartilaginous cap.

facts.statement: Caudal vertebrae feature tall, straight neural spines lacking the zygosphene-zygantrum joint common in most squamates.
facts.quote: The caudal vertebrae have tall, straight neural spines that lack any processes or zygosphene-zygantrum articulation, a joint found in most squamates.

facts.statement: The humerus is very short relative to its width, flattened in shape, and possesses a highly recurved elbow joint.
facts.quote: The humerus is very short in relation to its width, being flattened in shape and having a very recurved elbow joint.

facts.statement: The short, wide, and muscular humerus with paddle-shaped bones suggests Taniwhasaurus was an efficient swimmer.
facts.quote: This suggests that Taniwhasaurus would have had a muscular and powerful humerus that would have been short and wide, with paddle-shaped bones, indicating that it would have been an efficient swimmer.

facts.statement: In 1888, Lydekker reclassified Taniwhasaurus as a junior synonym of the genus Platecarpus.
facts.quote: In 1888, Taniwhasaurus was moved to the genus Platecarpus by Lydekker, considering it a junior synonym.

facts.statement: In 1971, Welles and Gregg placed Taniwhasaurus in the subfamily Tylosaurinae based on cranial similarities to Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: It was in 1971 that Taniwhasaurus was moved within the Tylosaurinae by Welles and Gregg, on the basis of cranial characteristics bringing it closer to the genus Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2019, Jiménez-Huidobro and Caldwell debated whether Taniwhasaurus is monophyletic, noting that some species have fossils too fragmentary for concrete assignment.
facts.quote: In 2019, in their phylogenetic review of this group, Jiménez-Huidobro and Caldwell believe that Taniwhasaurus cannot be considered with certainty to be monophyletic, because some named species have too fragmentary fossils to be assigned concretely to the genus.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Madzia and Cau suggests Taniwhasaurus evolved from Tylosaurus around 84 million years ago, implying a paraphyletic relationship.
facts.quote: A study published in 2020 by Daniel Madzia and Andrea Cau suggests a paraphyletic relationship of Tylosaurus, considering that Taniwhasaurus would have evolved from this latter, around 84 million years ago.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that the large snout foramina in Taniwhasaurus are correlated with its toothless snout, though this requires further validation.
facts.quote: This condition can be correlated with the toothless snout that characterizes the morphology of this subfamily, but further studies are needed to validate these two hypotheses.

facts.statement: T. antarcticus likely had a high capacity for lateral neck movement, but the muscles involved lacked significant strength.
facts.quote: T. antarcticus would therefore have had great capacity for lateral movement of the neck, although the muscles anchored there would not have had great strength.

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of Taniwhasaurus had a subcircular shape in the front that became ovoid and laterally compressed towards the back.
facts.quote: The terminal caudal vertebrae would support the caudal fin and, as in Plotosaurus, these have a subcircular section in the anterior region and turn into an ovoid shape compressed laterally posteriorly.

facts.statement: Researchers accept that the tail was the main source of propulsion for T. antarcticus, placing its swimming style between eel-like and carangiform forms.
facts.quote: Based on this evidence, it is accepted that although the entire vertebral column of T. antarcticus would have had great mobility, the tail would be the main source of propulsion, supporting the trend towards more carangiform forms, placing Taniwhasaurus somewhere between the forms eel-shaped basals and carangiform-derived forms.

facts.statement: Most species of Taniwhasaurus were endemic to the Weddellian Province of Gondwana, which included Antarctica, New Zealand, and Patagonia.
facts.quote: Excluding the species T. mikasaensis, the presence of T. oweni and T. antarcticus shows that the genus would have been endemic to Gondwana, and more specifically in the Cretaceous Austral Fauna of the Weddellian Province, a geographic area including Antarctica, New Zealand and Patagonia.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Southern Urals in Russia challenge the idea that Taniwhasaurus was endemic only to Gondwana.
facts.quote: However, the indeterminate tooth crown specimens identified as Taniwhasaurus sp. from the Santonian-aged strata of the Southern Urals in European Russia challenge the proposed Gondwanan endemism of this genus.

facts.statement: T. oweni fossils are found in the Conway Formation at Haumuri Bluff, dating to the Lower and Middle Campanian.
facts.quote: T. oweni is known from the Conway Formation, and more specifically from Haumuri Bluff, a locality containing Lower and Middle Campanian fossils.

facts.statement: The environment where T. oweni fossils were deposited was the lower zone of a foreshore.
facts.quote: The cores of the concretions present in the formation appear to be fossilized bones, shells or even wood, indicating that the environment of deposit would have been the lower zone of a foreshore.

facts.statement: T. antarcticus is known from Late Campanian deposits in the Snow Hill Island Formation on James Ross Island, Antarctica.
facts.quote: T. antarcticus is known from Late Campanian deposits of the Antarctic Peninsula, in the Snow Hill Island Formation, located on James Ross Island.

facts.statement: T. antarcticus fossils are primarily found in Member Gamma, a diverse site with marine and terrestrial fossils.
facts.quote: The taxon is known primarily from Member Gamma, a highly diverse site containing numerous fossils of marine and terrestrial faunas.

facts.statement: The type species T. oweni was named by Hector in 1874 based on fossils found in the Conway Formation at Haumuri Bluff, New Zealand.
facts.quote: Taniwhasaurus oweni, la especie tipo de Taniwhasaurus, fue nombrada por Héctor en 1874 a partir de un espécimen fósil hallado en estratos de la Formación Conway en Haumuri Bluff, Nueva Zelanda, que datan del Campaniano tardío.

facts.statement: T. oweni is estimated to have been at least 6 meters long based on the fossil remains.

facts.statement: In 2007, James E. Martin and Marta Fernández determined that Lakumasaurus was a junior synonym of Taniwhasaurus and recombined L. antarcticus as T. antarcticus.
facts.quote: Cuando el material tipo en 2007, James E. Martin y Marta Fernández determinaron que Lakumasaurus era un sinónimo más moderno de Taniwhasaurus y recombinaron la especie Lakumasaurus antarcticus como T. antarcticus.

facts.statement: The species T. mikasaensis was formally described by M.W. Caldwell et al. in 2008, though the name Yezosaurus mikasaensis was coined in 1977.
facts.quote: La "especie tipo", "Yezosaurus mikasaensis", fue acuñada por Obata y Muramoto en 1977, pero no fue formalmente descrita hasta 2008, cuando la especie T. mikasaensis fue descrita por M.W. Caldwell et al.

facts.statement: Taniwhasaurus was a close relative of the genera Tylosaurus and Hainosaurus.

facts.statement: Taniwhasaurus was a mosasaurid saurópsid that lived during the Late Cretaceous in New Zealand, Japan, and Antarctica.
